claim: A total of 1084 principal cells in the dorsal hippocampal CA1 were recorded using an array of 10 extracellular dodecatrodes in four well-trained rats.
source: A total of 1084 principal cells in the dorsal hippocampal CA1 were recorded using an array of 10 extracellular dodecatrodes (Takahashi and Sakurai, 2005) in four well-trained rats (individuals that had achieved an overall task performance of >90% for a week), while they were performing the task (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of cells recorded, the recording method, and the number of animals used.

claim: 556 place cells had spatial information >0.3 bits/spike and fired at significantly different rates during different trial types.
source: These cells, which had spatial information >0.3 bits/spike, fired at significantly different rates during different trial types (i.e., journey type and subtask), even when running speed, head direction, and x and y coordinates were taken into account (Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with these covariates, p < 0.05) (Wood et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific criteria for cell selection and statistical analysis results.

claim: The rats' paths could be accurately decoded from place cell activity sequences with median error of 6.0–13.5 cm.
source: For each trial type, the rats' paths could be accurately decoded from the place cell activity sequences (Figure 1C, top) using a memoryless Bayesian decoder (Figure 1C, middle; median error: 6.0–13.5 cm).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific decoding accuracy values and references Figure 1C showing the decoded paths.

claim: Trial type prediction accuracy during running was 74.3–84.5% overall mean across all rats.
source: Confusion matrices between predicted and actual trial types for each rat during the entire session (Figure 1D) show that a similar pattern was observed for all rats (overall mean, 74.3–84.5% (leave-one-out estimate), chance = 12.5%; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific prediction accuracy values and references Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: In correct trials, rats' heads pointed towards a goal in the opposite direction from the respective start zone.
source: In correct trials, the rats' heads pointed towards a goal in the opposite direction from the respective start zone (Watson–Williams test, P: 1.1 × 10−16, n = 588 (left), 1305 (right); Rayleigh test; P: left, 1.1 × 10−56, right, 4.9 × 10−324) and stem (Watson–Williams test, P: 1.1 × 10−16, n = 257 (left), 395 (right); Rayleigh test; P: left, 1.7 × 10−235, right, 5.2 × 10−125) (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 2 showing head direction data.

claim: Head direction was ambiguous in the maze stem during erroneous trials.
source: In erroneous trials, however, head direction was ambiguous only in the maze stem (Figure 2C,D; Watson–Williams test, (2C) P: 4.4 × 10−16, n = 29 (left), 30 (right), (2D) P: 0.29, n = 26 (left), 10 (right); Rayleigh test, P: (2C) left, 3.1 × 10−5, right, 8.2 × 10−18, (2D) left, 2.0 × 10−14, right, 5.1 × 10−7).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing non-significant head direction in the maze stem during errors.

claim: Of a total of 2820 candidate replays, 552 were identified as statistically significant replays with a continuous path.
source: Of a total of 2820 candidates, 552 were identified as statistically significant replays with a continuous path, whose length and duration satisfied several criteria (Davidson et al., 2009; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013) (see 'Materials and methods'; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of candidate and confirmed replays with references to methods and figures.

claim: 99.8% of LFPs during path replays were coincident with sharp wave/ripples.
source: LFPs during the path replays were largely coincident with the SWRs (99.8%; Table 2), and their theta power (4–12 Hz) was significantly smaller than during running (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage and references Table 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Path representation in the vicinity of both goals was significantly greater than in the remainder of the maze area.
source: Path representation in the vicinity of both goals was significantly greater than in the remainder of the maze area (Figure 4B; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 3.3 × 10−106, n = 552).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 4B.

claim: The median compression rate of place cell firing during replays was 9.0.
source: The median of the estimated compression rate was 9.0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that similarly to the timing of firing, place cell firing rates were also temporally compressed during replays.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific median value and references Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Path representation of future regions was significantly greater than that of past regions in correct spatial alternation trials.
source: Path representation (i.e., the sum total of the posterior probabilities of decoded locations) of future regions was significantly greater than that of past regions in the correct spatial alternation trials (Figure 5B; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.0037, n = 345).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 5B.

claim: Future regions were strongly and statistically significantly represented in correct visually guided trials.
source: Similarly, future regions were strongly and statistically significantly represented in the correct visually guided trials (Figure 5C,D; p = 0.0078, n = 52).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 5C,D.

claim: In erroneous trials, the difference between future and past path representation was not significant.
source: In erroneous trials, path representation of future regions was slightly greater than that of past regions (Figure 5E), but the difference was not significant (Figure 5F; p = 0.73, n = 9).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing non-significance.

claim: Path representation in path-stem replays on journeys toward an erroneous goal was significantly different from that on journeys toward a correct goal.
source: Surprisingly, however, path representation in path-stem replays on journeys toward an erroneous goal (Figure 5K) was significantly different from that on journeys toward a correct goal (Figure 5L; p = 0.0078, n = 8), despite the fact that the rats sampled both goal sides evenly.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 5K,L.

claim: Of the total 552 path replays, 108 were classified as episodic replays.
source: Accordingly, of the total 552 path replays, 108 were classified as episodic replays that satisfied criteria concerning the most frequently predicted trial type and its predicted probability sum (see 'Materials and methods'; Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers and references Table 2.

claim: The occurrence rate of episodic replays was significantly biased toward the DA subtask.
source: As expected, based on a previous study suggesting that awake SWRs support spatial working memory and not reference memory (Jadhav et al., 2012), the occurrence rate of overall episodic replays across all actual subtasks to be rewarded was significantly biased toward the DA subtask, which required spatial working memory (Figure 7A; Chi-square goodness-of-fit test, post hoc multiple binomial tests corrected by the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, VD vs DA: p = 8.6 × 10−5, NA vs DA: p = 9.9 × 10−4).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 7A and a previous study.

claim: The subtask bias occurred in episodic-start replays but not in episodic-stem replays.
source: The partitioning showed that the subtask bias occurred in episodic-start replays (Figure 7B; VD vs DA: p = 3.7 × 10−9; NA vs DA: p = 5.1 × 10−7), but not in episodic-stem replays (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 7B,C.

claim: Trial-type representation in episodic replays did not match the actual trial type in the start zones.
source: Trial-type representation in the episodic replays did not match the actual trial type in the start zones (Figure 7E; Choen's κ = 0.017; z test, p = 0.83, n = 71), but did match it in the stem (Figure 7F; Choen's κ = 0.31; p = 8.4 × 10−3, n = 34).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 7E,F.

claim: Trial-type representation matched actual trial type moderately well in replays at the junction.
source: Trial-type representation matched actual trial type moderately well in replays at the junction (i.e., the decision point) where the rats could evidently identify the actual trial type based on the visual cue (Figure 7H; Choen's κ = 0.58; p = 3.7 × 10−4, n = 17), but not at the center of the stem (Figure 7G; Choen's κ = 0.022; p = 0.93, n = 17).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 7G,H.

claim: The number of visual cues did not account for VD representation at the junction.
source: The number of visual cues showing did not account for VD representation, even at the junction (Figure 8A; χ2 test, p = 0.20).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing non-significance.

claim: The subtask predicted in the center of the stem did not match actual NA and DA trials.
source: However, the subtask predicted in the center of the stem did not match actual NA and DA trials (Figure 8B; χ2 test, p = 0.26).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing non-significance.

claim: The hippocampus is critically involved in episodic memory retrieval.
source: The hippocampus is critically involved in episodic memory retrieval, and within this structure reside place cells—principal cells exhibiting place-specific firing patterns in particular locations.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: Place cells exhibit place-specific firing patterns in particular locations.
source: The hippocampus is critically involved in episodic memory retrieval, and within this structure reside place cells—principal cells exhibiting place-specific firing patterns in particular locations.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about place cell properties.

claim: The hippocampus is the locus of the 'where' element of episodic memory.
source: The presence of such cells has led to the hypothesis that the hippocampus is the locus of the "where" element of episodic memory (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: Hippocampal place cell activity can represent odors and their match/non-match status in a particular location.
source: Following on from this seminal finding, more recent studies have demonstrated that hippocampal place cell activity simultaneously represents a broad range of aspects of memory, including odors and their match/non-match status in a particular location, called the "place field", as well as elapsed time (Otto and Eichenbaum, 1992; Sakurai, 1996; Wood et al., 1999; Pastalkova et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal place cell activity can represent elapsed time.
source: Following on from this seminal finding, more recent studies have demonstrated that hippocampal place cell activity simultaneously represents a broad range of aspects of memory, including odors and their match/non-match status in a particular location, called the "place field", as well as elapsed time (Otto and Eichenbaum, 1992; Sakurai, 1996; Wood et al., 1999; Pastalkova et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Place cell firing rate and location can change independently and are affected by external and internal factors.
source: In the place field, both firing rate and location can change independently and are affected by external factors, such as spatial environment and task demand, and internal factors such as prospective and retrospective memory (Markus et al., 1995; Frank et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2000; Anderson and Jeffery, 2003; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Smith and Mizumori, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: During maze running, place cell activity sequences convey information on both familiar paths and accompanying subtasks.
source: During maze running, place cell activity sequences in rodents convey information on both familiar paths and accompanying subtasks (Allen et al., 2012; Takahashi, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Place cell activity sequences are reactivated in a temporally compressed manner within sharp wave/ripples during slow-wave sleep or periods of awake immobility.
source: Within sharp wave/ripples (SWRs) in local field potentials (LFPs) during slow-wave sleep or periods of awake immobility, internally generated place cell activity sequences are often reactivated in a temporally compressed manner (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; O'Neill et al., 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Gupta et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: During brief periods of immobility, pivotal paths to a remembered goal can be predicted regardless of the location in which the SWRs have previously occurred.
source: During brief periods of immobility, pivotal paths to a remembered goal can be predicted, regardless of the location in which the SWRs have previously occurred (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013.

claim: Replay is considered a neuronal substrate for retrieving memories on familiar paths.
source: Such "replay" is thus considered a neuronal substrate for retrieving memories on familiar paths (Carr et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carr et al., 2011.

claim: Previous studies investigating the content of replays have primarily focused on the geography and timeline of the animals' running path.
source: However, previous studies investigating the content of replays have primarily focused on the geography and timeline of the animals' running path as experienced in the environment.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature.

claim: It is unclear whether replay conveys information on events occurring along the reactivated path.
source: It is therefore unclear whether the replay conveys information on events (i.e., "what" information) occurring along the reactivated path.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Differences between individual journeys are encoded in the firing locations of place cells.
source: I found that while the animal is running in the maze, differences between individual journeys and between subtasks in the maze are independently encoded in the firing locations and rates of place cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the author's previous study (Takahashi, 2013).

claim: Differences between subtasks are encoded in the firing rates of place cells.
source: I found that while the animal is running in the maze, differences between individual journeys and between subtasks in the maze are independently encoded in the firing locations and rates of place cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the author's previous study (Takahashi, 2013).

claim: All trial types experienced in the maze could be decoded from the ensemble activity of place cells during running.
source: Furthermore, all trial types (i.e., journey type and subtask) experienced in the maze could be decoded from the ensemble activity of place cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the author's previous study (Takahashi, 2013).

claim: Four rats were trained for about one hour in a specific sequence of subtasks.
source: According to the subtask switching protocol, four rats were trained for about one hour in a specific sequence—VD (20 laps), NA (20 laps), VD (10 laps), DA (20 laps), VD (20 laps), NA (20 laps), VD (10 laps), and DA (20 laps)—and were rewarded each time they arrived at the reward zone at the correct return rail (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: In the VD subtask, a cue light indicated which direction to turn at the decision point to receive a reward.
source: In the VD subtask, a cue light on the left or right side was illuminated to indicate which direction to turn at a decision point (Figure 1A) to receive a reward.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: In both NA and DA subtasks, rats had to alternate between left and right at the decision point.
source: In both the NA and DA subtasks, cue lights on both sides were illuminated and the rats had to alternate between left and right at the decision point (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: The difference between NA and DA subtasks was that DA imposed a 5-second delay period with a barrier in the middle of the central stem.
source: The difference between the NA and DA subtasks was that in the DA subtask, a barrier appeared in the middle of the central stem for five seconds to impose a delay period.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: The subtask to be rewarded could only be distinguished at the decision point based on visual cues.
source: The subtask to be rewarded (i.e., VD, NA, or DA) could therefore only be distinguished at the decision point, based on visual cues (Takahashi, 2013).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the task design.

claim: The Bayesian decoder and prediction method together are sufficient for interpreting the representation of path and trial type in place cell activity sequences.
source: The Bayesian decoder and the prediction method together are sufficient for interpreting the representation of path and trial type in place cell activity sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation analyses during running.

claim: Rats sampled a memory-guided goal in preparation for switching to either the NA or DA subtask.
source: In correct trials, the rats' heads pointed towards a goal in the opposite direction from the respective start zone (Watson–Williams test, P: 1.1 × 10−16, n = 588 (left), 1305 (right); Rayleigh test; P: left, 1.1 × 10−56, right, 4.9 × 10−324) and stem (Watson–Williams test, P: 1.1 × 10−16, n = 257 (left), 395 (right); Rayleigh test; P: left, 1.7 × 10−235, right, 5.2 × 10−125) (Figure 2). This suggests that the rats sampled a memory-guided goal in preparation for switching to either the NA or the DA subtask.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the head direction data.

claim: Head direction is a behavioral sign indicating expected future choice.
source: In this experiment, head direction is therefore considered a behavioral sign indicating expected future choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the head direction analyses.

claim: Prior to making erroneous choices, rats did not make a decision at the behavioral level within the maze stem.
source: Considering that the barrier in the maze stem would have been an indication to the rats of the ongoing DA subtask, this suggests that the spatial memory demand in preparation for NA/DA subtasks decreased within the maze stem. In addition, prior to making erroneous choices, the rats did not make a decision at the behavioral level within the maze stem.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ambiguous head direction during erroneous trials.

claim: Path replays predominantly occurred in the start zone and in the maze stem.
source: The path replays predominantly occurred in the start zone and in the maze stem (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of replays shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The path replays were not a simple consequence of either reward expectation or place-specific firings in the location where they occurred.
source: This suggests that the path replays were not a simple consequence of either reward expectation or place-specific firings in the location where they occurred (Gupta et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis showing no correlation with occupancy time or place-field representation.

claim: Path replays may represent paths on a memory-guided journey towards an upcoming goal or on the immediately preceding journey.
source: Rather, they may represent paths on a memory-guided journey towards an upcoming goal (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013), or on the immediately preceding journey (O'Neill et al., 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and supported by citations.

claim: In the maze stem where spatial memory retrieval is a prerequisite for predicting a future goal, path representation in the replay is directly linked to the animal's future path.
source: Similar to the findings of a previous study (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013), this suggests that in the maze stem, where spatial memory retrieval is a prerequisite for predicting a future goal, path representation in the replay is directly linked to the animal's future path.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of path-stem replays and supported by citation.

claim: The upcoming path encoded in the awake replay can be linked to the animal's future actions.
source: My findings strongly support this view, with the additional finding that the upcoming path encoded in the awake replay can be linked to the animal's future actions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of replays during correct and erroneous trials.

claim: The maximum firing rates of place cells during replays were about 10 times faster than typical maximum firing rates during running.
source: As expected from the timing of temporally compressed firings across place cells, the maximum firing rates of place cells during replays (∼80 Hz) were about 10 times faster than typical maximum firing rates during running (∼8 Hz).
evidence: This is a comparison of firing rates between running and replay periods.

claim: Place cell firing rates were temporally compressed during replays.
source: The median of the estimated compression rate was 9.0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that similarly to the timing of firing, place cell firing rates were also temporally compressed during replays.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the compression rate analysis.

claim: The firing rates of neurons participating in the replay may contain information on the differences between subtasks.
source: However, the firing rates during DARL trials were substantially greater than during VDRL trials, suggesting that the firing rates of neurons participating in the replay may contain information on the differences between subtasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences in firing rates between subtasks.

claim: Awake SWRs support spatial working memory and not reference memory.
source: As expected, based on a previous study suggesting that awake SWRs support spatial working memory and not reference memory (Jadhav et al., 2012), the occurrence rate of overall episodic replays across all actual subtasks to be rewarded was significantly biased toward the DA subtask, which required spatial working memory
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited to support the interpretation of the current findings.

claim: The bias towards DA subtask cannot be explained by the time spent pausing.
source: However, since the rats specifically spent more time pausing in the DA subtask in both the start zones and the maze stem (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E), the bias cannot be explained by the time spent pausing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of pause times across subtasks.

claim: The occurrence rate of replays is enhanced by upcoming spatial working memory demand.
source: Combined with behavioral signs of decreased spatial memory demand within the maze stem, these results suggest that the occurrence rate of replays is enhanced by upcoming spatial working memory demand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of replay occurrence rates across subtasks and locations.

claim: The enhancement of replays is not specifically due to the reactivated DA subtask, but instead due to the reactivation of all previously experienced subtasks.
source: This suggests that the enhancement is not specifically due to the reactivated DA subtask, but instead due to the reactivation of all previously experienced subtasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis showing that predicted subtasks reflected the ratio of experienced subtasks.

claim: Trial-type representation in the replays is more than just a representation of external cues and is internally generated.
source: This suggests that trial-type representation in the replays is more than just a representation of external cues, and that it is internally generated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analyses showing that visual cues and barriers did not account for trial-type representation.

claim: The internally generated replay represents the actual trial type when the trial type can be identified, but otherwise it evenly represents all trial types thus far experienced on the reactivated path.
source: I therefore conclude that the internally generated replay represents the actual trial type—not only the upcoming path but also the actual subtask to be rewarded—when the trial type can be identified, but otherwise it evenly represents all trial types thus far experienced on the reactivated path.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the analyses.

claim: The replay can represent non-spatial information on subtask as well as spatial information concerning the path.
source: Firstly, the replay can represent non-spatial information on subtask as well as spatial information concerning the path.
evidence: This is one of the main findings summarized in the Discussion.

claim: The path in the replay is encoded in temporally compressed firing timings across place cells, while the accompanying subtask is encoded in their temporally compressed firing rates.
source: Secondly, whereas the path in the replay is encoded in temporally compressed firing timings across place cells, the accompanying subtask is encoded in their temporally compressed firing rates.
evidence: This is one of the main findings summarized in the Discussion.

claim: The replay is enhanced by spatial working memory demand.
source: Thirdly, the replay is enhanced by spatial working memory demand.
evidence: This is one of the main findings summarized in the Discussion.

claim: Global and rate remapping mechanisms during running are preserved in the temporally compressed replays that occur during brief periods of immobility.
source: I have now shown that replays also encode non-spatial information in temporally compressed firing rates, revealing that global and rate remapping mechanisms during running (Leutgeb et al., 2005; Takahashi, 2013) are preserved in the temporally compressed replays that occur during brief periods of immobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Awake replay is more common in a novel environment.
source: Since awake replay is more common in a novel environment (Cheng and Frank, 2008), a few previous studies (O'Neill et al., 2006) have speculated that the content of replays reflects the total of previous experience.
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies cited in the Discussion.

claim: Replays are not a simple function of experience.
source: Contradicting with this hypothesis, growing evidence suggests that replays are not a simple function of experience (Gupta et al., 2010), but rather that reward outcomes enhance the reactivation of experiences (Singer and Frank, 2009) and that replays can depict future paths to remembered goals (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies cited in the Discussion.

claim: Reward outcomes enhance the reactivation of experiences.
source: Contradicting with this hypothesis, growing evidence suggests that replays are not a simple function of experience (Gupta et al., 2010), but rather that reward outcomes enhance the reactivation of experiences (Singer and Frank, 2009) and that replays can depict future paths to remembered goals (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies cited in the Discussion.

claim: Replays can depict future paths to remembered goals.
source: Contradicting with this hypothesis, growing evidence suggests that replays are not a simple function of experience (Gupta et al., 2010), but rather that reward outcomes enhance the reactivation of experiences (Singer and Frank, 2009) and that replays can depict future paths to remembered goals (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies cited in the Discussion.

claim: Awake replays often begin at the animal's current location.
source: In addition, awake replays often begin at the animal's current location (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the Discussion.

claim: Awake replay is similar to vicarious trial-and-error (VTE) events.
source: Some previous reports suggest that awake replay is similar to vicarious trial-and-error (VTE) events (Hu and Amsel, 1995; Johnson and Redish, 2007), because it can represent possible future paths even in completely unfamiliar places (Gupta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies cited in the Discussion.

claim: Awake replay associated with SWRs is seen frequently at the choice point where animals must make a memory-guided decision between two journeys.
source: Although VTE events are reported to occur outside of SWRs, a subsequent study suggested that awake replay associated with SWRs is seen frequently at the choice point in a similar task, where animals must make a memory-guided decision between two journeys (Karlsson and Frank, 2009).
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the Discussion.

claim: Replays provide information on possible upcoming paths to downstream brain structures which can assess the value of different paths and make a decision about future actions.
source: Frank et al. therefore proposed a unified interpretation in which replays provide information on possible upcoming paths to downstream brain structures such as the prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens, which can assess the value of different paths and make a decision about future actions (Carr et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study cited in the Discussion.

claim: Not only the path but also the subtask representation in the replay is similar to VTE events.
source: However, the task design did not allow prediction of the subtask until the animal had entered the decision point. This suggests that not only the path but also the subtask representation in the replay is similar to VTE events.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of VTE.

claim: Replays prepare the brain for unforeseen changes, which would allow continuous switching between subtasks.
source: By extending the unified interpretation to include non-spatial memory in the retrieved memory, the fact that replays in the present study reflected all previously experienced trial types (except at the decision point) suggests that replays prepare the brain for unforeseen changes, which would allow continuous switching between subtasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings extending previous hypotheses.

claim: The initiation of an awake replay is often related to external spatial input at the animal's location.
source: Since the initiation of an awake replay is often related to external spatial input at the animal's location (Karlsson and Frank, 2009), this enhancement of replays suggests that the internal demand of the hippocampal-dependent spatial working memory is another factor.
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the Discussion.

claim: Awake replay plays a key role in episodic-like memory retrieval, which contributes to memory-based navigational planning and decision making.
source: Considering that this is similar to a cued memory retrieval process, my findings strongly support the hypothesis that awake replay plays a key role in episodic-like memory retrieval, which contributes to memory-based navigational planning and decision making (Carr et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings and supported by citation.

claim: Sequential activation of place cell activity associated with SWRs can represent paths where the animal has never experienced.
source: The sequential activation of place cell activity associated with SWRs can also represent paths where the animal has never experienced (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Dragoi and Tonegawa 2013a; 2013b; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies cited in the Discussion.

claim: A fairly large proportion of events representing different and multiple experiences can spontaneously occur, even in naive animals.
source: As a result, a fairly large proportion of events representing different and multiple experiences can spontaneously occur, even in naive animals.
evidence: This is a claim about preplay events based on cited literature.

claim: Paths and subtasks were encoded in temporally compressed firing timings and rates, respectively, in the replays to arrange multiple preplayed episodes into a single replay event.
source: I speculate that the reason why paths and subtasks were encoded in temporally compressed firing timings and rates, respectively, in the replays may be to arrange such multiple preplayed episodes into a single replay event to easily recall and imagine an upcoming episode based on prior experience.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The training protocol might have helped to recruit a consistent path representation across the three subtasks.
source: In the present study, the rats were sequentially trained in the VD, NA, and DA subtasks. Together with the preplay mechanism, this training protocol might have helped to recruit a consistent path representation across the three subtasks.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the training protocol may have influenced the results.

claim: Non-spatial information in the preplay may provide further insight into memory encoding and retrieval.
source: Until now, previous studies investigating the content of preplays have primarily focused on the geography and timeline of the animals' running. Non-spatial information in the preplay may provide further insight into memory encoding and retrieval.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the current findings.

claim: Awake replay is linked to the typical abilities of episodic memory: mental time travel and foreseeing future situations.
source: I therefore speculate that awake replay is linked to the typical abilities of episodic memory: mental time travel and foreseeing future situations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The findings provide novel insight into debates on animals' capacities to use the faculties provided by episodic memory.
source: This provides novel insight into debates on animals' capacities to use the faculties provided by episodic memory (Allen and Fortin, 2013).
evidence: This is a claim about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: Rats were housed individually in cages where the light was maintained in a 12-hr light–dark cycle.
source: Four male Wistar rats implanted with a custom-made microdrive were housed individually in cages where the light was maintained in a 12-hr light–dark cycle.
evidence: This describes the housing conditions for the animals.

claim: Tests were performed during the light phase.
source: The tests were performed during the light phase.
evidence: This describes when the experiments were conducted.

claim: The weight of all rats was kept at 80% of free-feeding body weight.
source: The weight of all rats was kept at 80% of free-feeding body weight.
evidence: This describes the weight maintenance protocol.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Doshisha University and Kyoto Sangyo University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees.
source: All procedures were approved by the Doshisha University and Kyoto Sangyo University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees.
evidence: This states the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Rats achieved at least 80% correct decisions for >20 laps in the VD subtask before training in the NA subtask.
source: The rats were trained until they achieved at least 80% correct decisions for >20 laps. Next, they were trained to perform the NA subtask for >20 laps.
evidence: This describes the training criteria.

claim: Rats achieved a 90% correct decision rate from the beginning of the DA subtask.
source: The rats paused reliably, facing the forward direction, in front of the barrier, and achieved a 90% correct decision rate from the beginning of this task.
evidence: This describes the performance in the DA subtask.

claim: The task was performed under dim light to prevent rats from receiving any unintended distal room cues.
source: To prevent the rats from receiving any unintended distal room cues, the task was performed under dim light.
evidence: This describes a control measure in the experimental design.

claim: Rats did not receive the visual cue until they reached the decision point because the height of the walls was much higher than the level of the rat's eyes.
source: They did not receive the visual cue until they reached the decision point because the height of the walls of the maze (20 cm) was much higher than the level of the rat's eyes (∼5 cm) and they did not stand up during the experiment.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design ensuring task control.

claim: The sole signal for subtask switching was LEDs that were visible only at the decision point.
source: The sole signal for subtask switching was therefore LEDs that were visible only at the decision point.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Stimulation electrodes were inserted into the MFB in the right lateral hypothalamus at coordinates AP 2.5, ML 1.0, DV 9.5.
source: Under isoflurane anesthesia, stimulation electrodes were inserted into the MFB in the right lateral hypothalamus (AP 2.5, ML 1.0, DV 9.5).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure and electrode placement.

claim: A custom-made microdrive with 10 independently movable dodecatrodes was fixed to the skull above the left hippocampus at coordinates AP 3.8, ML 3.0, DV 0.5.
source: A custom-made microdrive with 10 independently movable dodecatrodes was then fixed to the skull above the left hippocampus (AP 3.8, ML 3.0, DV 0.5).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure and electrode placement.

claim: Electrodes were individually lowered into the pyramidal cell layer of the hippocampal CA1 a week after surgery.
source: A week after surgery, the electrodes were individually lowered into the pyramidal cell layer of the hippocampal CA1.
evidence: This describes the post-surgical procedure.

claim: Extracellular signals were unity-gain buffered, filtered (600 Hz–6 kHz), amplified (gain = 5000), and continuously sampled at 25 kHz.
source: The extracellular signals were unity-gain buffered, filtered (600 Hz–6 kHz), amplified (gain = 5000), and continuously sampled at 25 kHz.
evidence: This describes the signal processing parameters.

claim: LFP recordings were filtered (0.1 Hz–6 kHz) and amplified (gain = 500).
source: One channel of each electrode was duplicated for detecting LFPs and was filtered (0.1 Hz–6 kHz) and amplified (gain = 500).
evidence: This describes the LFP recording parameters.

claim: LFP recordings were further band-pass filtered (150–250 Hz) using the Hilbert transform for SWR detection.
source: The LFP recordings were further band-pass filtered (150–250 Hz) using the Hilbert transform.
evidence: This describes the signal processing for SWR detection.

claim: Local peaks in the power of filtered signal of magnitude >mean + 3SD were identified as SWR events during periods when running speed was <2 cm/s.
source: Local peaks in the power of this filtered signal of magnitude >mean + 3SD were identified and extracted as periods. The boundaries for each period were defined as the point at which the amplitude crossed the mean. Periods during which running speed was <2 cm/s were identified as SWR events.
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying SWR events.

claim: Putative principal cells were distinguished from putative fast-spiking cells based on spike width (0.4 ms) and average firing rate (5 Hz).
source: After spike sorting as previously described (Takahashi et al., 2003; Takahashi and Sakurai, 2009; Takahashi, 2013), putative principal cells were distinguished from putative fast-spiking cells based on spike width (0.4 ms) and average firing rate (5 Hz).
evidence: This describes the criteria for cell classification.

claim: Cells whose firing rate was <0.1 Hz were excluded.
source: Cells whose firing rate was <0.1 Hz were excluded.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for cells.

claim: Spikes during delay periods in the DA subtask were excluded because hippocampal activity was not place-specific during these periods.
source: Spikes during delay periods in the DA subtask, when hippocampal activity was not place-specific (Pastalkova et al., 2008), were excluded.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion and is supported by citation.

claim: Spatial bins had a resolution of approximately 2 cm for place map construction.
source: Spatial bins had a resolution of approximately 2 cm.
evidence: This describes a parameter for place map construction.

claim: Place maps were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 3-cm width.
source: A one-dimensional map of the place field for each place cell was then constructed for each trial type in the standard manner (Takahashi, 2013) (smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 3-cm width).
evidence: This describes a parameter for place map construction.

claim: Place maps were constructed from spikes only when running speed was >5 cm/s.
source: The place map was constructed from spikes only when running speed was >5 cm/s so that spikes generated while the rats paused in front of the barrier wall in the DA subtask were excluded.
evidence: This describes a criterion for place map construction.

claim: Time windows for task performance and replays were set at 250 ms and 20 ms, respectively, for Bayesian decoding.
source: Time windows for task performance and replays were set at 250 ms and 20 ms, respectively.
evidence: This describes parameters for the Bayesian decoder.

claim: A candidate replay was defined as a period where the smoothed population activity was greater than the mean and the peak was above mean + 3SD.
source: A candidate replay was defined as a period where the smoothed (Gaussian kernel; SD: 10 ms) population activity was greater than the mean and the peak was above the defined threshold (mean + 3SD).
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying candidate replays.

claim: Time windows for candidate replays were reduced such that at least 10% of all detected cells were detected within the time window, each cell included at least two spikes, and the duration was at least 30 ms.
source: To minimize ambiguous detections, periods were decreased based on the following criteria. Time windows were reduced as much as possible such that at least 10% of all detected cells were detected within the time window, each cell included at least two spikes, and the duration was at least 30 ms.
evidence: This describes the criteria for refining candidate replays.

claim: For Bayesian decoding of replays, locations were decoded for 20-ms time windows advanced in 5-ms increments.
source: Secondly, for each period, the rat's location was decoded using the Bayesian decoder, for 20-ms time windows advanced in 5-ms increments.
evidence: This describes parameters for the Bayesian decoder during replay analysis.

claim: Periods were concatenated when the distance between neighboring decoded locations was less than 25 cm.
source: Periods were concatenated when the distance between neighboring decoded locations was less than 25 cm.
evidence: This describes a criterion for concatenating replay periods.

claim: Concatenated periods whose sequence of decoded locations covered a total distance greater than that covered during four time windows were classified as candidate replays.
source: Thirdly, concatenated periods whose sequence of decoded locations covered a total distance greater than that covered during four time windows were classified as candidate replays.
evidence: This describes a criterion for classifying candidate replays.

claim: Two significance tests were conducted for every candidate using a Monte Carlo method with cell identity and cell place field shuffling (5000 times each).
source: Fourthly, two significance tests were conducted for every candidate, using a Monte Carlo method with two different random shuffling modes: cell identity and cell place field (5000 times each).
evidence: This describes the statistical testing procedure for replays.

claim: Candidates with p < 0.05 for both shuffle modes were defined as path replays.
source: Finally, candidates with p < 0.05 for both shuffle modes were defined as path replays.
evidence: This describes the criterion for defining path replays.

claim: Binary population vectors were constructed based on whether each cell's firing rate in 200-ms time windows was higher or lower than its mean firing rate for the whole session.
source: Firstly, a binary population vector, C, was constructed. This vector could exist in one of two states, high or low. The state was determined on the basis of 200-ms time windows throughout the entire session, based on whether the cell's firing rate in each time window was higher or lower than its mean firing rate for the whole session.
evidence: This describes the method for constructing binary population vectors.

claim: Path replays with p < 0.05 for both cell identity and decoded location shuffle modes were defined as episodic replays.
source: Significance tests were conducted using a Monte Carlo method with two random shuffling modes: cell identity and decoded location (5000 times each). The path replays with p < 0.05 for both shuffle modes were defined as episodic replays.
evidence: This describes the criterion for defining episodic replays.

claim: All analyses were performed using custom-made programs based on Matlab (v8.3; MathWorks) and R functions.
source: All analyses were performed using custom-made programs based on Matlab (v8.3; MathWorks) and R (R Development Core Team, 2013) functions.
evidence: This describes the software used for analysis.
